name: High-shelf filter

semantics.definition: A filter response that applies a signed gain difference to the high-frequency side of a transition region relative to the low-frequency side, with both sides approaching plateaus.

evidence.claim: Defines high shelf by the high-frequency side while signed shelf gain remains a separate parameter and documents a hybrid product counterexample.
Documents the related term high shelving filter and separate boost-or-cut behavior.
Documents a compact High Shelf type selector with gain, slope, and Q controlled separately.
Documents an independent compact High Shelf type selector without establishing shared geometry.
Defines a highshelf implementation token whose affected side is invariant across signed gain.
Provides dated educational use of High-shelf with a separate Boost/Cut value.
Defines high shelf as boost or cut above cutoff and separates positive and negative illustrative states.
Shows that response-curve orientation alone does not identify shelf side without gain context.
Documents an axis-free, sign-agnostic high-shelf selector that forks on the high-frequency right side while signed gain remains separate.
Provides historical independent use of the same affected-side two-prong high-shelf topology with separate gain.
Documents a third independent mirrored two-prong high-shelf selector with separate gain.
Preserves a polarity-dependent single-curve shelf implementation as counterevidence to universal form.
Directly maps High Shelf controls to the high shelving filter response class while gain and Q remain separate parameters.
Uses high-shelf and high-shelving forms within one API operation while gain, slope, cutoff, and type remain separate inputs.
Independently uses the exact high-shelving filter phrase with separate gain control.
Connects the highshelf machine name to a two-pole shelving-filter class without establishing global treble or concatenated-token aliases.
Independently confirms the parameterized highShelf response family without proving the shelving morphology by itself.
Preserves a product-local highpass enum for shelf-side selection as adverse evidence against global pass-term transfer.
Preserves the collision-prone framework phrase high-pass shelf filter as product-local wording outside exact aliases.
Shows polarity- and topology-specific high shelving controls that defeat implementation equivalence while preserving response-class terminology.

confidence.rationale: Affected-side semantics, full-name text communication, shelf-specific overlap review, and cross-vendor two-prong topology convergence are well supported; isolated recognition and portable glyph interchange remain unresolved.

open_questions.question: Is high shelving filter an exact alias at the bounded response-class level documented by DA-022?
Do independent compact implementations converge on a reproducible sign-agnostic high-shelf primitive?
Which Unicode characters, sequences, and adjacent-standard symbols overlap or conflict with this concept?
Does isolated use reliably distinguish the high-shelf topology from low-pass in the six-member family?

notes: The ASCII identifier is provisional until registry-accepted.
Boost versus attenuation, gain sign and amount, plateau placement, slope, order, Q, resonance, overshoot, implementation, and UI context are excluded from semantic identity.
High cut is not an alias; it collides with the existing low-pass terminology boundary.
HS, HSF, treble shelf, and signed boost/cut names are not adopted as aliases or fallbacks.
High shelving filter is an exact alias only for the high-shelf response class; it carries no gain-sign, parameter, topology, control, implementation, algorithm, or glyph equivalence.

Shelf versus shelving is a morphological relationship, not an orthographic variant. Whole-label lookup may fold ASCII case and normalize one internal ASCII space or attributive hyphen without adding duplicate aliases; concatenated or camel-case tokens are not inferred.
High shelving remains a related fragment. Plain shelving filter, plain shelf filter, treble, highpass, high-pass shelf filter, HS, HSC, and signed boost/cut names remain outside exact global aliases.
Explicit product documentation overrides generic alias lookup when it assigns a different, narrower, compound, polarity-specific, or otherwise product-local operation.
The independently established topology forks on the high-frequency right side and converges toward the unaffected left side; signed gain remains separate.
Affected-side orientation is semantic: the high-shelf form forks on the high-frequency right side. Arbitrary rotation or mirroring that changes the forked side is not equivalent.
Axes, baselines, parameter values, slope, color, interaction state, exact proportions, path curvature, whitespace, line weight, and endpoint placement are not semantic identity.
The two-prong convention is convergent, not universal; polarity-bearing single curves and contextual alternatives remain documented counterevidence.
The representative glyph concept does not accept or publish artwork.
